title: China stalls Nvidia H200 imports to boost domestic AI chips
summary: China stalls Nvidia H200 imports to boost domestic AI chips
detailed: Approximately 600,000 Nvidia H200 AI chips are currently stored in Hong Kong because the Chinese government has not approved large-scale imports.

While U.S. export controls permit the sales, China is restricting large-scale inflows to protect its domestic chip industry, allowing limited purchases primarily for AI model training rather than service inference.
Server asking prices for systems equipped with eight H200 chips in mainland China surged past 6 million yuan in the unofficial gray market.
This matters because the intersection of U.S. export rules and Chinese import restrictions creates supply bottlenecks and rising hardware costs for major Chinese AI tech firms.
sentences: About 600,000 of Nvidia's artificial intelligence (AI) chips are reportedly piled up in Hong Kong, unable to enter mainland China.
The U.S. government allowed exports, but China has not approved large-scale imports.
China's big tech companies need high-performance U.S. chips to develop AI models, but the Chinese government is wary of rising dependence on U.S. technology.
Policies aimed at protecting the domestic chip industry are instead becoming an obstacle for Chinese AI companies to secure chips.

On the 5th (local time), Reuters, citing two sources familiar with the matter, reported that about 600,000 of Nvidia's high-performance AI Semiconductor H200 chips are being stored in Hong Kong, unable to be brought into mainland China.
This is the first time the specific quantity of H200s stacked in Hong Kong has been reported.
The Chinese government has in recent months allowed the entry of some H200s.
Several major Chinese internet companies are each said to have secured about 10,000 H200s.
Small quantities have also come in through brokers or indirect channels.

However, authorities are still not approving large-scale imports.
◇ Need U.S. chips, but protecting domestic industry comes first
This situation stems from the overlap of U.S. export controls and China's chip self-sufficiency policy.
Since 2022, the United States has restricted China's access to advanced AI Semiconductors and chipmaking equipment.
The move aimed to keep China's advanced technology development in check.
The H200 had been subject to the U.S. export ban, but the Donald Trump administration changed policy after last year's U.S.-China trade talks to allow sales to approved Chinese customers.
Separately, the Chinese government is maintaining its own import restrictions.
If large volumes of U.S. chips flow in, domestic companies may keep choosing Nvidia products, which outperform Chinese-made offerings.
That could clash with policy goals for Chinese chipmakers to expand their market and build technological capabilities.
It is in the same vein that China is not completely blocking U.S. chips.

In AI model training, which is hard to replace immediately with Chinese products, U.S. chips are allowed on a limited basis, while in deploying AI models in actual services, the aim is to increase the use of Chinese chips.

Earlier, the information technology (IT) outlet The Information reported in July that authorities had notified Alibaba, ByteDance Ltd., and DeepSeek that they could allow limited purchases of H200s for AI model training.
The Information said total approved volume could come in under 200,000 units.
China is said to have required that domestic chips be used first for "inference," which deploys AI models in actual services.
AI model training is the process of processing vast amounts of data to improve a model's performance.
Inference is the task of using a trained model to answer questions or generate outputs.

The view is that by distinguishing training from inference to manage chip use, the Chinese government aims to secure the performance needed for AI development while growing the domestic chip market.
◇ The paradox of technological self-reliance: burden in securing high-performance chips
The problem is that Chinese chips still do not fully match the performance of Nvidia's products.
The H200 is not Nvidia's latest AI Semiconductor, but it is evaluated as offering performance that Chinese substitutes have not caught up to.
It is especially useful for training large-scale AI models when combined with Nvidia's software.
As major Chinese tech companies such as Alibaba, ByteDance Ltd., and Tencent expand AI services, demand is also rising for high-performance chips like the H200.
The drive by China's big tech firms to secure other U.S.-made chips is related to this demand.
Reuters reported last month that ByteDance Ltd., Alibaba, and Tencent ordered more than 3 million of Nvidia's RTX Pro 5500 graphics cards.

The product is less powerful than the H200 but complies with U.S. export rules, and the list prices for the order volume total more than $35 billion (about 47 trillion won).
◇ Server asking prices surge in the gray market amid import limits
In particular, as U.S. export controls and China's import limits intersect, prices are surging in the unofficial chip market.
According to Reuters, at the end of Oct., a server equipped with eight H200 chips in mainland China was offered for sale at more than 6 million yuan (about 1.2 billion won).
That is about triple the price a year earlier.
Servers equipped with Nvidia's next-generation Blackwell chips, which are subject to U.S. export controls, were reportedly offered at more than 20 million yuan (about 4 billion won) per unit.
Analysts say China's chip self-reliance policy could raise development costs for domestic AI companies in the short term.
If imports are restricted when Chinese chips cannot fully replace Nvidia's products, securing high-performance chips could become even harder.
Depending on whether the government approves large-scale imports in the future, Chinese AI companies' chip supply and development costs are also expected to be affected.
